translation: The Du meridian arises at Huiyin, follows the back, and runs behind the body; being the chief governor of the yang vessels, it is therefore called the Sea of the Yang Vessels. The Ren meridian arises at Huiyin, follows the abdomen, and runs in front of the body; being that which undertakes and bears (chengren) the yin vessels, it is therefore called the Sea of the Yin Vessels. The Chong meridian arises at Huiyin, flanks the navel as it runs, and rushes straight upward; being the crucial thoroughfare of the various vessels, it is therefore called the Sea of the Twelve Meridians. The Dai meridian, on the other hand, encircles the waist transversely with a form like a girdle, and so it is the one that binds together all the vessels. For this reason the Yang Wei governs the entire exterior of the body, and the Yin Wei governs the entire interior of the body — this is spoken of in terms of Qian and Kun (heaven and earth). The Yang Qiao governs the yang of the left and right of the body, and the Yin Qiao governs the yin of the left and right of the body — this is spoken of in terms of east and west.
